claim: TCF7L1 is an embryonic stem cell signature gene that is upregulated in multiple aggressive cancer types.
source: TCF7L1 is an embryonic stem cell signature gene that is upregulated in multiple aggressive cancer types, but its role in skin tumorigenesis has not yet been defined.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ben-Porath et al., 2008 in the Introduction section

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression increases tumor incidence in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
source: Here we document TCF7L1 upregulation in skin squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and demonstrate that TCF7L1 overexpression increases tumor incidence, tumor multiplicity, and malignant progression in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,E,H showing tumor incidence curves

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression increases tumor multiplicity in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
source: Here we document TCF7L1 upregulation in skin squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and demonstrate that TCF7L1 overexpression increases tumor incidence, tumor multiplicity, and malignant progression in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,F showing average number of tumors per mouse

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression increases malignant progression in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
source: Here we document TCF7L1 upregulation in skin squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) and demonstrate that TCF7L1 overexpression increases tumor incidence, tumor multiplicity, and malignant progression in the chemically induced mouse model of skin SCC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D,G,J showing percentage of mice with SCC

claim: Downregulation of TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 reduces tumor growth in a xenograft model of human skin SCC.
source: Additionally, we show that downregulation of TCF7L1 and its paralogue TCF7L2 reduces tumor growth in a xenograft model of human skin SCC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D showing reduced tumor mass

claim: TCF7L1 promotes tumor growth independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
source: Using separation-of-function mutants, we show that TCF7L1 promotes tumor growth, enhances cell migration, and overrides oncogenic RAS-induced senescence independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating that TCF7L1ΔN (lacking β-catenin binding domain) increases tumor size similarly to full-length TCF7L1

claim: TCF7L1 enhances cell migration independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
source: Using separation-of-function mutants, we show that TCF7L1 promotes tumor growth, enhances cell migration, and overrides oncogenic RAS-induced senescence independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 demonstrating that TCF7L1ΔN increases cell migration similarly to full-length TCF7L1

claim: TCF7L1 overrides oncogenic RAS-induced senescence independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
source: Using separation-of-function mutants, we show that TCF7L1 promotes tumor growth, enhances cell migration, and overrides oncogenic RAS-induced senescence independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D demonstrating that TCF7L1ΔN suppresses HRAS-induced senescence similarly to full-length TCF7L1

claim: LCN2 is a major downstream effector of TCF7L1 that drives tumor growth.
source: Through transcriptome profiling and combined gain- and loss-of-function studies, we identified LCN2 as a major downstream effector of TCF7L1 that drives tumor growth.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10E,F demonstrating that downregulating LCN2 abrogates the effect of TCF7L1 overexpression on tumor growth

claim: TCF7L1 is upregulated in DMBA/TPA-induced mouse papillomas.
source: Although TCF7L1 expression is normally restricted to the bulge and outer root sheath cells of the hair follicle and is absent in the interfollicular epidermis, we observed widespread expression in papillomas and even greater expression in skin SCC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A

claim: TCF7L1 is upregulated in DMBA/TPA-induced mouse skin SCC.
source: Although TCF7L1 expression is normally restricted to the bulge and outer root sheath cells of the hair follicle and is absent in the interfollicular epidermis, we observed widespread expression in papillomas and even greater expression in skin SCC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A

claim: TCF7L1 expression is normally restricted to the bulge and outer root sheath cells of the hair follicle in normal skin.
source: Although TCF7L1 expression is normally restricted to the bulge and outer root sheath cells of the hair follicle and is absent in the interfollicular epidermis, we observed widespread expression in papillomas and even greater expression in skin SCC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A and cited literature (DasGupta and Fuchs, 1999; Merrill et al., 2001; Nguyen et al., 2006)

claim: TCF7L1 is absent in the interfollicular epidermis in normal skin.
source: Although TCF7L1 expression is normally restricted to the bulge and outer root sheath cells of the hair follicle and is absent in the interfollicular epidermis, we observed widespread expression in papillomas and even greater expression in skin SCC (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1A

claim: TCF7L1 expression is increased in 2 out of 4 cases of UV-induced mouse skin SCC examined.
source: In the UV-induced mouse model of skin SCC, where papillomas and SCC develop from skin that is chronically exposed to UV radiation, increased expression of TCF7L1 was also observed in 2 out of 4 cases of skin SCC examined (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Under high-dose DMBA/TPA treatment, TCF7L1-induced mice developed a greater number of papillomas at a faster rate than control mice.
source: Under a high-dose DMBA (100 nmol) and TPA (10 nmol) treatment, TCF7L1-induced mice developed a greater number of papillomas at a faster rate than control mice did (Figure 2B,C; n = 17 TCF7L1-induced, n = 16 control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C

claim: Progression to SCC occurred at a higher frequency and faster rate in TCF7L1-induced animals under high-dose DMBA/TPA treatment.
source: Progression to SCC also occurred at a higher frequency and faster rate in the TCF7L1-induced animals (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D

claim: Under low-dose DMBA/TPA treatment, 80% of TCF7L1-induced animals formed papilloma compared to less than 20% of control animals.
source: In contrast to control animals that experienced a lower than 20% frequency of tumor formation, 80% of TCF7L1-induced animals formed papilloma and 60% developed SCC (Figure 2E–G; n = 16 TCF7L1-induced, n = 21 control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E

claim: Under low-dose DMBA/TPA treatment, 60% of TCF7L1-induced animals developed SCC.
source: In contrast to control animals that experienced a lower than 20% frequency of tumor formation, 80% of TCF7L1-induced animals formed papilloma and 60% developed SCC (Figure 2E–G; n = 16 TCF7L1-induced, n = 21 control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The size of tumors did not differ significantly between control and TCF7L1-induced groups.
source: The size of the tumors, however, did not differ significantly between the control and TCF7L1-induced groups (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in text but data not shown

claim: Prolonged overexpression of TCF7L1 in adult skin results in hyperproliferation of the stratified epidermis and hair follicle.
source: Here we found that prolonged overexpression of TCF7L1 in adult skin results in hyperproliferation of the stratified epidermis and hair follicle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Expression of Ki67 did not change after five days of TCF7L1 induction.
source: Whereas expression of the proliferative marker Ki67 did not change after five days of TCF7L1 induction, Ki-67 was detected throughout the interfollicular epidermis and the hair follicle after one month of TCF7L1 induction.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Ki-67 was detected throughout the interfollicular epidermis and the hair follicle after one month of TCF7L1 induction.
source: Whereas expression of the proliferative marker Ki67 did not change after five days of TCF7L1 induction, Ki-67 was detected throughout the interfollicular epidermis and the hair follicle after one month of TCF7L1 induction.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: TCF7L1-induced epidermis shows aberrant expression of Keratin 6 (KRT6) in the suprabasal layer.
source: In the suprabasal layer of the TCF7L1-induced epidermis, we found aberrant expression of Keratin 6 (KRT6), which normally marks the inner layer of the hair follicle but is also induced in hyperproliferative cells at the wound edge, as well as hyperplastic, neoplastic, and psoriatic epidermis (Moll et al., 1982; Weiss et al., 1984; Stoler et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and cited literature

claim: Hair follicle cells in TCF7L1-induced skin are more proliferative after one month of induction as shown by increased Ki67 staining.
source: After one month of TCF7L1 induction, hair follicle cells in the TCF7L1-induced skin are more proliferative as shown by increased Ki67 staining and altered hair follicle morphology (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: Hair follicles in TCF7L1-induced skin are elongated after one month of induction, illustrating growth.
source: In contrast to the quiescent and short hair follicles in the control skin, the hair follicles in TCF7L1-induced skin are elongated, illustrating growth.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence and H&E data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B,D

claim: Over 30% of TCF7L1-induced mice developed papilloma when treated with DMBA alone (without TPA).
source: We found that while almost none of the control mice developed tumors, over 30% of the TCF7L1-induced mice developed papilloma (Figure 2H–J; n = 22 TCF7L1-induced, n = 26 control).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: TCF7L1 can act as a tumor promoter, substituting for pro-inflammatory TPA application in the DMBA/TPA chemical carcinogenesis protocol.
source: That the DMBA/acetone treated TCF7L1-induced mice developed tumors at a similar rate to the DMBA/TPA treated control mice (Figure 2E–J) suggests that TCF7L1 can act as a tumor promoter, since its expression was able to substitute for pro-inflammatory TPA application in the DMBA/TPA chemical carcinogenesis protocol.
evidence: Supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2E-J

claim: TCF7L1 is overexpressed in a majority of human skin SCC cell lines.
source: We found that TCF7L1 is overexpressed in a majority of human skin SCC cell lines (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Knocking down TCF7L1 only modestly reduced tumor growth in xenografted SCC13 cells.
source: We found that knocking down TCF7L1 only modestly reduced tumor growth while knocking down both TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 significantly reduced the tumor size (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Knocking down both TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 significantly reduced xenografted tumor size.
source: We found that knocking down TCF7L1 only modestly reduced tumor growth while knocking down both TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 significantly reduced the tumor size (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Silencing TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 reduces SCC cell proliferation in vitro.
source: Consistent with the observation that silencing TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 reduced tumor size, their downregulation reduced SCC cell proliferation in vitro and in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by MTT assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: Silencing TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 reduces SCC cell proliferation in vivo.
source: Consistent with the observation that silencing TCF7L1 and TCF7L2 reduced tumor size, their downregulation reduced SCC cell proliferation in vitro and in vivo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Ki67 immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression significantly increased the average mass of xenografted tumors derived from SRB12 cells.
source: At the end point of the experiment, we measured the average mass of TCF7L1-overexpressing tumors and found it was significantly greater than that of the control tumors. TCF7L1 overexpression increased the weight of xenografted tumors derived from both skin SCC cell lines, SRB12 (Figure 4A) and SCC13 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression increased the weight of xenografted tumors derived from SCC13 cells.
source: At the end point of the experiment, we measured the average mass of TCF7L1-overexpressing tumors and found it was significantly greater than that of the control tumors. TCF7L1 overexpression increased the weight of xenografted tumors derived from both skin SCC cell lines, SRB12 (Figure 4A) and SCC13 (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TCF7L1-overexpressing SCC cells form tumors at a higher efficiency in limiting dilution assay.
source: We also tested the tumorigenic ability of TCF7L1-overexpressing SCC cells by grafting transduced cells at limiting dilution onto immunodeficient mice. We found that TCF7L1-overexpressing cells form tumors at a higher efficiency (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Tumors expressing induced myc-TCF7L1 display increased proliferation as evident by higher level of BrdU incorporation.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of xenografted tumors showed that tumors expressing induced myc-TCF7L1 display increased proliferation, evident by the higher level of BrdU incorporation (Figure 4C, upper panel) and increased number of Ki67-positive cells (Figure 4C, lower panel, and Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C upper panel

claim: Tumors expressing induced myc-TCF7L1 display increased number of Ki67-positive cells.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of xenografted tumors showed that tumors expressing induced myc-TCF7L1 display increased proliferation, evident by the higher level of BrdU incorporation (Figure 4C, upper panel) and increased number of Ki67-positive cells (Figure 4C, lower panel, and Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4C lower panel and quantification in Figure 4D

claim: TCF7L1ΔN (lacking β-catenin binding domain) increased tumor size similarly to full-length TCF7L1.
source: Notably, the β-catenin binding-deficient TCF7L1ΔN mutant increased tumor size similarly to full-length TCF7L1, whereas the Groucho/TLE corepressor binding-deficient TCF7L1ΔG did not significantly increase the tumor size (despite having a 100 fold stronger activity on WNT reporter in vitro).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TCF7L1ΔG (lacking Groucho/TLE binding domain) did not significantly increase tumor size.
source: Notably, the β-catenin binding-deficient TCF7L1ΔN mutant increased tumor size similarly to full-length TCF7L1, whereas the Groucho/TLE corepressor binding-deficient TCF7L1ΔG did not significantly increase the tumor size (despite having a 100 fold stronger activity on WNT reporter in vitro).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TCF7L1* (which cannot bind to DNA) had little effect on tumor size.
source: We found that full-length TCF7L1 overexpression significantly increased tumor size relative to the control while TCF7L1*, which cannot bind to DNA, had little effect (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TCF7L1 does not require binding to β-catenin to promote human skin SCC tumor growth.
source: These data indicate that TCF7L1 does not require binding to β-catenin to promote human skin SCC tumor growth and suggest that TCF7L1 might act as a co-repressor in its tumor-promoting role.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating TCF7L1ΔN has similar effect as full-length TCF7L1

claim: TCF7L1 might act as a co-repressor in its tumor-promoting role.
source: These data indicate that TCF7L1 does not require binding to β-catenin to promote human skin SCC tumor growth and suggest that TCF7L1 might act as a co-repressor in its tumor-promoting role.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TCF7L1ΔG (lacking Groucho/TLE binding) does not increase tumor size while TCF7L1ΔN does

claim: Expression of oncogenic HRASG12V induces senescence in primary mouse keratinocytes.
source: As expected, expression of oncogenic HRASG12V-induced senescence in both primary mouse keratinocytes (Figure 6A–C) and fibroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6A-C

claim: Expression of oncogenic HRASG12V induces senescence in fibroblasts.
source: As expected, expression of oncogenic HRASG12V-induced senescence in both primary mouse keratinocytes (Figure 6A–C) and fibroblasts (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: TCF7L1 co-expression significantly reduced the effect of oncogenic HRASG12V on senescence in keratinocytes.
source: However, when co-expressed with TCF7L1, its effect on senescence in keratinocytes was significantly reduced (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6A-C

claim: TCF7L1 counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence independently of its binding to β-catenin.
source: Importantly, TCF7L1 counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence independently of its binding to β-catenin, as TCF7L1ΔN mutant exerted even greater negating effect than full-length TCF7L1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6D

claim: TCF7L1ΔN mutant exerted even greater negating effect on HRASG12V-induced senescence than full-length TCF7L1.
source: Importantly, TCF7L1 counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence independently of its binding to β-catenin, as TCF7L1ΔN mutant exerted even greater negating effect than full-length TCF7L1 (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6D

claim: Oncogene-induced senescence was not affected by the overexpression of ΔNβ-catenin.
source: Consistent with our finding that TCF7L1 suppressed OIS independently of β-catenin, we found that OIS was not affected by the overexpression of ΔNβ-catenin, the N-terminus truncated version of β-catenin that is hyper-active due to its increased stability and consequent nuclear localization (Gat et al., 1998) (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2A

claim: Introducing ΔNβ-catenin together with TCF7L1 reduced the suppressing effect of TCF7L1 on oncogene-induced senescence.
source: In fact, introducing ΔNβ-catenin together with TCF7L1 reduced the suppressing effect of TCF7L1 on OIS.
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6E

claim: TCF7L1 acts independently of ΔNβ-catenin to suppress HRASG12V-induced senescence.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that TCF7L1 acts independently of ΔNβ-catenin to suppress HRASG12V-induced senescence.
evidence: Supported by SA-β-gal activity data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2

claim: TCF7L1 stimulates migration of SCC13 cells.
source: Using the Boyden chamber assay, we confirmed that TCF7L1 also stimulates cell migration in two different human SCC cell lines, SCC13 and SRB12 (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 7A,B

claim: TCF7L1 stimulates migration of SRB12 cells.
source: Using the Boyden chamber assay, we confirmed that TCF7L1 also stimulates cell migration in two different human SCC cell lines, SCC13 and SRB12 (Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 7C

claim: A significant increase in motility was observed in SCC cells expressing full-length TCF7L1.
source: We observed a significant increase in motility in cells expressing full-length TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN, with little change upon TCF7L1ΔG expression.
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: A significant increase in motility was observed in SCC cells expressing TCF7L1ΔN.
source: We observed a significant increase in motility in cells expressing full-length TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN, with little change upon TCF7L1ΔG expression.
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: Little change in motility was observed upon TCF7L1ΔG expression in SCC cells.
source: We observed a significant increase in motility in cells expressing full-length TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN, with little change upon TCF7L1ΔG expression.
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 7B,C

claim: TCF7L1 stimulated migration of skin SCC cells independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
source: Thus, as with its role in promoting tumor growth and suppressing oncogene-induced senescence, TCF7L1 stimulated migration of skin SCC cells independently of its interaction with β-catenin.
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data showing TCF7L1ΔN has similar effect as full-length TCF7L1 in Figure 7

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L2 increased xenografted SCC tumor size.
source: Importantly, overexpression of TCF7L2 also increased xenografted SCC tumor size, accelerated cell migration, and counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence (Figure 8) similarly as TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L2 accelerated cell migration.
source: Importantly, overexpression of TCF7L2 also increased xenografted SCC tumor size, accelerated cell migration, and counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence (Figure 8) similarly as TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8B,C

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L2 counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence.
source: Importantly, overexpression of TCF7L2 also increased xenografted SCC tumor size, accelerated cell migration, and counteracted HRASG12V-induced senescence (Figure 8) similarly as TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D

claim: TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN share a similar altered gene signature.
source: Gene expression heatmaps of these transduced cells illustrate that indeed TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN share a similar altered gene signature.
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 9A

claim: 359 genes were induced (≥2 fold) by both TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN but not by TCF7L1*.
source: Venn diagrams constructed with gene sets that were significantly altered (Q < 0.05) in three groups identified 359 genes that were induced (≥2 fold) and 43 genes that were repressed (≥2 fold) by both TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN but not by TCF7L1* (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 9B

claim: 43 genes were repressed (≥2 fold) by both TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN but not by TCF7L1*.
source: Venn diagrams constructed with gene sets that were significantly altered (Q < 0.05) in three groups identified 359 genes that were induced (≥2 fold) and 43 genes that were repressed (≥2 fold) by both TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN but not by TCF7L1* (Figure 9B).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 9B

claim: The top three induced GO biological processes by TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN were inflammation, response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to molecule of bacterial origin.
source: Among the listed GO biological processes (p<0.05), the top three induced GO terms were inflammation, response to lipopolysaccharide, and response to molecule of bacterial origin.
evidence: Supported by GO term analysis shown in Figure 9C

claim: The top three induced KEGG pathways by TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN were genes involved in complement and coagulation cascades, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, and TNF signaling pathway.
source: Among the listed KEGG pathways (p<0.05), the top three induced GO terms were genes involved in complement and coagulation cascades, cytokine-cytokine receptor interaction, and TNF signaling pathway.
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis shown in Figure 9C

claim: LCN2 is among the top 20 significantly induced genes by TCF7L1 and TCF7L1ΔN but not TCF7L1*.
source: Inflammation-related factors such as LTA, RRAD, LCN2 and TNF were included in the top 20 significantly induced gene list (Q < 0.05) (Figure 9D,E).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 9D,E

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN increased expression of LCN2 more significantly than the overexpression of TCF7L1ΔG in SCC13 cells.
source: In both SCC13 and SRB12 human SCC cell lines, we verified by real time PCR that overexpression of either TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN increased expression of LCN2 more significantly than the overexpression of TCF7L1ΔG, while overexpression of TCF7L1* had little effect (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN increased expression of LCN2 more significantly than the overexpression of TCF7L1ΔG in SRB12 cells.
source: In both SCC13 and SRB12 human SCC cell lines, we verified by real time PCR that overexpression of either TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN increased expression of LCN2 more significantly than the overexpression of TCF7L1ΔG, while overexpression of TCF7L1* had little effect (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1* had little effect on LCN2 expression.
source: In both SCC13 and SRB12 human SCC cell lines, we verified by real time PCR that overexpression of either TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN increased expression of LCN2 more significantly than the overexpression of TCF7L1ΔG, while overexpression of TCF7L1* had little effect (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR data shown in Figure 10A

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 induced expression of LCN2 in vivo.
source: We showed that overexpression of TCF7L1 induced expression of LCN2 in vivo (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) as previously reported (Miao et al., 2014) and that expression of LCN2 was also induced in murine skin papilloma and SCC (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B) similarly to TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1A and cited literature (Miao et al., 2014)

claim: Expression of LCN2 was induced in murine skin papilloma.
source: We showed that overexpression of TCF7L1 induced expression of LCN2 in vivo (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) as previously reported (Miao et al., 2014) and that expression of LCN2 was also induced in murine skin papilloma and SCC (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B) similarly to TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10B and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B

claim: Expression of LCN2 was induced in murine skin SCC.
source: We showed that overexpression of TCF7L1 induced expression of LCN2 in vivo (Figure 10—figure supplement 1A) as previously reported (Miao et al., 2014) and that expression of LCN2 was also induced in murine skin papilloma and SCC (Figure 10C, Figure 10—figure supplement 1B) similarly to TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by RT-PCR and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10B and Figure 10—figure supplement 1B

claim: 10 out of 16 human skin SCC samples were positive for TCF7L1.
source: Through immunostaining of human skin samples (n = 16), we found that while 10 out of 16 samples were positive for TCF7L1, 15 were positive for LCN2 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: 15 out of 16 human skin SCC samples were positive for LCN2.
source: Through immunostaining of human skin samples (n = 16), we found that while 10 out of 16 samples were positive for TCF7L1, 15 were positive for LCN2 (Figure 10—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: All TCF7L1 expressing human skin SCC tumors express LCN2.
source: In addition, although all of TCF7L1 expressing tumors express LCN2, 83.3% of TCF7L1 negative also express LCN2, indicating that LCN2 can be induced by factors other than TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: 83.3% of TCF7L1 negative human skin SCC tumors also express LCN2.
source: In addition, although all of TCF7L1 expressing tumors express LCN2, 83.3% of TCF7L1 negative also express LCN2, indicating that LCN2 can be induced by factors other than TCF7L1.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 2

claim: LCN2 can be induced by factors other than TCF7L1.
source: In addition, although all of TCF7L1 expressing tumors express LCN2, 83.3% of TCF7L1 negative also express LCN2, indicating that LCN2 can be induced by factors other than TCF7L1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TCF7L1-negative tumors also express LCN2

claim: Downregulating LCN2 decreased tumor size, abrogating the effect of TCF7L1 overexpression on tumor growth.
source: After eight weeks, TCF7L1-overexpressing tumors were significantly bigger than the control tumors. Importantly, downregulating LCN2 decreased tumor size, abrogating the effect of TCF7L1 overexpression on tumor growth (Figure 10E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 10E,F

claim: Inhibition of LCN2 with neutralizing antibody abolished the promigratory effect of TCF7L1 in SCC cells.
source: Moreover, as was similarly shown in primary murine keratinocytes (Miao et al., 2014), inhibition of LCN2 with neutralizing antibody abolished the promigratory effect of TCF7L1 in SCC cells (Figure 10G).
evidence: Supported by Boyden chamber assay data shown in Figure 10G and cited literature (Miao et al., 2014)

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 did not affect the number of macrophages in xenografted tumors.
source: We found that while overexpression of TCF7L1 did not affect the number of macrophages (vector: 2.78 ± 1.57% vs. TCF7L1: 2.27 ± 1.02%), it increased the number of neutrophils by four fold (vector: 0.36 ± 0.09% vs. TCF7L1: 2.28 ± 0.74%).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3D

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 increased the number of neutrophils by four fold in xenografted tumors.
source: We found that while overexpression of TCF7L1 did not affect the number of macrophages (vector: 2.78 ± 1.57% vs. TCF7L1: 2.27 ± 1.02%), it increased the number of neutrophils by four fold (vector: 0.36 ± 0.09% vs. TCF7L1: 2.28 ± 0.74%).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 3C

source: Since overexpression of TCF7L1 increased papilloma incidence but not papilloma size, we postulate that TCF7L1 facilitates the transformation of mutated cells into premalignant state and contributes little to growth of papilloma.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TCF7L1 does not increase papilloma size

claim: Overexpression of TCF7L1 stimulates the progression of papilloma into malignancy.
source: Moreover, since TCF7L1-induced mice developed more SCCs, we speculate that overexpression of TCF7L1 also stimulates the progression of papilloma into malignancy.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that TCF7L1-induced mice developed more SCCs

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression did not stimulate proliferation of DMBA/TPA induced papilloma per se.
source: Since overexpression of TCF7L1 did not stimulate proliferation of DMBA/TPA induced papilloma per se and did not promote tumor development without DMBA treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), it suggests that TCF7L1 may facilitate the transitioning of DMBA-induced mutated cells into premalignant tumors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C

claim: TCF7L1 may facilitate the transitioning of DMBA-induced mutated cells into premalignant tumors.
source: Since overexpression of TCF7L1 did not stimulate proliferation of DMBA/TPA induced papilloma per se and did not promote tumor development without DMBA treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C), it suggests that TCF7L1 may facilitate the transitioning of DMBA-induced mutated cells into premalignant tumors.
evidence: Inferred from observations about TCF7L1's effects in different experimental conditions

claim: TCF7L1 overexpression transforms the global gene expression profile of SCC cells.
source: Our transcriptome analyses of SCC cells expressing TCF7L1 or its mutant variants found that overexpression of TCF7L1 or TCF7L1ΔN transforms the global gene expression profile to a similar extent (Figure 9A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 9A

claim: TCF7L1 discovered a causative link between TCF7L1 up-regulation and cancer-associated inflammation in skin tumorigenesis.
source: Our study discovered a causative link between TCF7L1 up-regulation and cancer-associated inflammation in skin tumorigenesis, suggesting that TCF7L1 may facilitate tumor growth through induction of a subset of cytokines in a paracrine manner.
evidence: Inferred from RNAseq data showing inflammatory genes are induced by TCF7L1
